blocks.label: Cancer as a genetic disease and the role of the microenvironment
blocks.content: [background chatter] Okay, good afternoon, everybody. We'll get started now on this second of the cancer lectures. So I'm Suzanne Turner. I'm Professor of Childhood Cancer Biology in the Department of Pathology. And as well as having a research group that investigates mechanisms of childhood cancer, my other job is to teach you guys. And of course, some of you have met me through the practical classes. And together with Professor Leman, we're going to give you the lectures on cancer. So this course of six lectures, the second of which today, we're going to think about what causes cancer. So you've seen in your first lecture and in the practical classes that cancer is this growing mass of cells that acquires this ability to invade into underlying tissue spaces. So what allows cells to pick up the properties that enable them to do that? And so within this lecture, hopefully by the end of it, you'll be suitably, educated so that you can appraise evidence linking environmental exposures with cancer development, that you can summarize the methodologies we use to determine the carcinogenicity of environmental exposures, and that you'll be able to discuss the relative roles of cancer initiators and promoters in the development of malignancies. So what is cancer? So at its heart, it's a genetic disease, right? It's a disease whereby cells in our body pick up mutations over time, and we know that cancer is generally a disease that we see in an older population. So that fits with a lifetime of acquiring mutations in your cells. And those mutations largely are repaired by our DNA repair machinery. But sometimes, those mutations perhaps give an advantage to the cell, a clonal advantage, an evolutionary advantage, and perhaps those cells are able to continue to proliferate and pass on those mutations to their progeny. And ultimately, over time, pick up sufficient mutations that allow them to acquire all the properties that they need to become invasive growths. But is it that simple? Is it just a matter of picking up mutations in a cell, in genes that control cell cycle and proliferation, and then growing out as a big mass? Well, of course, nothing in life is ever that simple, and it's certainly not the case with cancer. And as you would have seen by looking at the slides in your practical classes, and for the NATscis, I appreciate your classes this afternoon, there are all sorts of other cells in there amongst the tumor cells. There's a blood supply. The cells need nutrients. They need factors to enable them to grow and proliferate. They're not completely autonomous for growth. We know there are inflammatory cells in there, and here you saw this mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Whether that's reacting to a tumor antigen or an opportunistic infection, we don't know, but we know there are inflammatory cells there. We know there are lots of stromal cells there providing support. So it's not just the mass of cells picking up mutations and growing out. There also has to be a permissive microenvironment. But ultimately, at its core, we have a collection of cells, or maybe starting with one cell, that picks up mutations in key genes which enable them to acquire new properties, and we call these properties the hallmarks of cancer, and we'll come onto these at a later lecture. So cells have to pick up properties which mean they're able to grow and invade into underlying tissue spaces. And of course, we have to remember that cancer is essentially evolution occurring on a micro scale. And there will be clones of cells that have perhaps a competitive advantage over their neighbors due to the mutations and the genes in which those mutations occur. And there might not be one route to the development of cancer, and we know this is a collection of hundreds, if not thousands, of different diseases because we're all genetically distinct. We're all info-- exposed to different environmental factors. And it is ultimately evolution. So the conditions will have to be just right for these masses to grow out. And of course, we know that 50% of us will develop cancer in our lifetimes. So the risks are quite high.
blocks.topicLabel: Cancer development, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns

blocks.label: Endogenous processes, inherited predisposition, and target cell types
blocks.content: So what is driving that? What is going on that enables that to happen? And this is where I'm going to introduce you to my roulette wheel of cancer. Because there are a number of things we do on a daily basis which expose our DNA to carcinogens, to mutagens, which potentially tip the balance towards cell acquiring mutations and perhaps properties that enable them to grow and invade. And of course, we know that there are lots of endogenous processes that do that. So we think just the process of metabolism in cells produces reactive oxygen species that can damage DNA. We know, for example, that some cells inherently undergo DNA mutations when we think about B cells and somatic hypermutation, for example. We know that when cells are rapidly dividing, it's very hard for those DNA repair mechanisms to keep up with the damage that's done as we're replicating our genome, sometimes under very stressful conditions. And so there are situations our bodies go under where we're under extreme stress, where there may be inflammation, when these processes are perhaps occurring at a rate that's too fast for our DNA repair processes to keep up with. So at these stages, perhaps we're inherently predisposed to picking up mutations that may happen in genes that control key cell cycle checkpoints, key properties of cells which are controlling their growth. Okay. So there is an element of bad luck, you might say, that these mutations may occur and they may occur in important genes. We may repair the damage, we may not repair the damage. But of course also, we expose ourselves to all sorts of things in our environment which we know are also carcinogenic. And of course, these are the things that you've been taught from a very young age when you went to primary school and had to wear sunscreen, because we know UV light is associated with skin cancer. We know that smoking cigarettes causes lung cancer. So there are lots of things we do that we know we shouldn't do, which tip the balance in the favor of picking up mutations which may happen in important genes. And then we have some people who perhaps inherit a predisposition, are genetically predisposed. So you can imagine a scenario, if you inherit a DNA repair deficiency syndrome, your ability to repair DNA damage is reduced, you're at a higher risk of developing cancer. And there are also families that inherit mutations in key cell cycle checkpoint proteins such as Li-Fraumeni families, where they all inherit mutations in P53, that key cell cycle checkpoint protein, and you do see throughout the family history incidences of cancer. There are also other cancers where, for example, there's a childhood cancer called retinoblastoma, where children inherit, well, they've essentially lost one copy of retinoblastoma. They're born with just one copy of the gene, and this is classic two-hit hypothesis, where they only then have to lose that second allele, and therefore then they lose this key checkpoint protein which is controlling their cells. So there is some inherited predisposition, but it's a very small percentage of all cancer cases overall. And the other thing we might want to think about is the cell that these mutations are occurring in. And you could imagine that if those mutations are occurring in terminally differentiated cells, it's perhaps of no consequence because those cells are destined to die, unless those mutations are in genes which control the process of apoptosis, for example. But if your mutations occur in a long-lived stem cell, that's a cell that's also hanging around long enough to pick up more mutations as we age. And the more mutations we pick up, the greater the chances they'll be in those key proteins that control cell cycle and proliferation. Those mutations may also occur in a cell that then enables them to reacquire stemness properties. So there's all sorts of scenarios you could imagine whereby cancer might develop. And you'll notice I use the term a lot, perhaps, maybe, because ultimately, we don't know. We can come up with hypotheses, we can come up with frameworks by which we can try and understand cancer cell biology, but there's always going to be an exception. But what we're teaching you in these lectures is to try and teach you some rules so we can start to think about the concepts surrounding cancer cell biology.
blocks.topicLabel: Cancer development, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns

blocks.label: Known and emerging environmental carcinogens
blocks.content: And so I'm going to think a little bit about those environmental mutagens now. And of course, this one is really clear. We all know this one, right? If you smoke cigarettes, you get lung cancer. There's a clear association between an exposure and a specific type of cancer. So it doesn't take too much of a brain to figure out what might be going on there, and of course, cigarettes are full of carcinogens, and we'll talk about some of those today. Then there are environmental exposures, things that perhaps we thought were safe, but then it turns out many years later that they weren't. An example of that, of course, being asbestos. Now, asbestos is not a mutagen. It can't mutate your DNA. It happens in a different way to change DNA in cells, and we're going to come onto that example as well. Bye. [laughs] So, of course, asbestos is pretty safe, so don't worry about it too much as long as it's not broken and the fibers are released, and you'll appreciate that in a couple of slides' time. Sunbeds, UV light. We all know about that too, right? If you sit out in the sun, if you use sunbeds, higher risk of skin cancer. And then there are things we don't know about. So there are lots of cases of ovarian cancer occurring in women who've used talcum powder. Turns out that in the production of this talcum powder, there was some asbestos creeping in in the production process. Lots of legal cases going on, as you can imagine. Weed killer. Turns out a lot of people are exposed to weed killer in their occupation, gardeners and so on, were developing lymphoma. And we think that's because at the time that Roundup was manufactured, it was made and it had a constituent chemical called glyphosphate, which is a mutagen. It's banned now from pesticides. But that's what was going on. So often we don't learn about these things until much later. People that were chronically using Zantac started developing a range of different cancers. Turns out that was contaminated with a chemical called NMDA, that's also a mutagen. Again, you can imagine, lots of legal cases, particularly in the US. What about hormone replacement therapy? Hormones, they're safe, right? Hormones are being produced in our body naturally. Why would hormone replacement therapy cause cancer? And actually, a lot of this came from epidemiological studies, some of them weaker than others. And since it's been shown that perhaps the risk isn't quite as high as we think, but this tells us that some cancers are still reliant on hormones for growth. So they're not completely autonomous. But we also have to think medically about the risks, the balance. How does a woman feel when she's not on hormone replacement therapy? And is the risk of breast cancer perhaps too low to consider that that might be something to stop you doing that? So again, there are lots of factors that come into these things. There are things that maybe you think are safe that really aren't. So a new cancer is emerging that rises in the context of women who have breast implants. It's a very specific type of breast implant manufactured by just a couple of companies, and they've been developing a lymphoma in their breast, not a breast cancer, a lymphoma. What is it about this breast implant that's causing cancer? And that's the story we hope to solve in our lab. And then there are things we're exposed to that we really don't know if they're carcinogenic. And one example I'm giving you here are microplastics. So we all drink bottles of water. They're full of microplastics. We consume about a credit card's worth of microplastics every day. They're in the water. They're in our fish. They're in the Antarctic. Could these be mutagenic? There's no evidence quite yet, but we're working on that.
blocks.topicLabel: Cancer development, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns

blocks.label: The 'bad luck' vs environment debate and public perception
blocks.content: So ultimately, we spend our lives with our cells endogenously undergoing processes which are error-prone. We're exposing ourselves to lots of things in the environment which we know can cause mutations. And I always like to think a little bit about public understanding of science when we think about this. And there was this couple of essays that were written by Tomassetti and Vogelstein, so quite a while ago now. But they wrote a couple of papers in a very prominent journal, where they suggested that actually you could put cancers down to two factors. Most of them are due to bad luck. So just these inherent processes that are going on in our bodies. We pick up mutations. Some are repaired, some aren't. Some happen in genes which are no functional consequence. Some happen in important cell cycle control genes. But ultimately, there's not much we can do about it. And then they put some down to environmental exposure. So these are generally the things you think about. Some of them are associated with exposure to pathogens. Some are exposed to radiation. Some are cigarette smoke and lung cancer. And I like this quote here, "There is a mystery here. I don't think even Professor Doll could elucidate it." So Professor Doll was the guy, the epidemiologist, who first put the link together between cigarette smoking and lung cancer. "The mystery of the thousands of people who had smoked like chimneys without coming to any harm". And we all hear about those people, right? They lived till they were 102. They smoked 60 cigarettes a day. They had a bottle of whiskey every week. But they did a bit of Tai Chi or something like that, and they lived. They didn't get cancer. So is it really random and down to bad luck? Well, I suggest there's a bit of a balance there, and you can do a lot to tip the balance in the other direction. Just for a bit of fun, a few quotes here that came up on the Daily Mail website in response to the public interpretation of this paper. So good old Flavius there in Italy thinks it's now safe to smoke in front of his kids because the chances of developing cancer, it's just bad luck, right? Not a lot we can do about that. Another one here, as I was talking about before, "My grandad's 98, smoked for 30 years. But then he gave up, and he started doing Tai Chi and walking very fast and eating ginger and garlic". So does ginger and garlic counteract the effects of cigarette smoke? Maybe. Who knows? And then I like this one as well, the conspiracy theorists. "Who wants to cure cancer?" I'm a cancer scientist. Why would I want to put myself out of a job? Why would those drug companies want to cure cancer? Because they'd go out of business. Anyway, cancer, is it inevitable or is it caused? And again, I think there's a balance of things there we have to think about that we're going to think about today.
blocks.topicLabel: Cancer development, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns

blocks.label: Geographical variation and epidemiology in cancer incidence
blocks.content: And a lot of studies that have been done to try and link causes to cancer outcomes are largely epidemiological studies. So a lot of the evidence that we have to begin with, such as those studies which link cigarette smoking to lung cancer, came from epidemiology. And epidemiology has its place, of course, but there are lots of cool things you can do with statistics to make your epidemiological study look in whatever way you want. There's lots of caveats. There's lots of confounders. So every time we interpret an epidemiological study, we have to bear those things in mind. But I'm going to highlight this study here, which basically looked at different types of cancer that we saw in different regions around the world. And these are age standardized incidences, and I'm going to point out a couple of things here. So breast and prostate cancer. Now, the highest rate of breast and prostate cancer is in the US. The lowest rates are in China and Israel. Why is that? Is it environmental? Is it genetic? And we know, of course, that there are BRCA families, so there are people who are inherited predispositions. And actually, you'll notice there it says non-Jews because the Ashkenazi Jews inherit BRCA mutations. There's a long family lineage of that. So they do have high rates of breast cancer. But what's happening in the US to give them high rates of these hormone-related cancers? Is it the bad diet? Is it the environment? Are they genetically predisposed? Another example here, colon, melanoma. Colon cancer again is really high in the USA but really low in India. Is it diet? Lots of fast food. Lots of obesity. I'm generalizing here, of course. But could that be part of the problem? Whereas perhaps in India, maybe spicy foods, and again, I'm generalizing. Does that protect against cancer? Melanoma, well, why wouldn't it be higher in Australia? Very sunny place, lots of exposure to the sun. Lowest in Japan. Do they maybe protect themselves a bit more from the sun? Carry parasols? I don't know. But there are clear epidemiological differences there. Couple of others I'll point out. Stomach and liver cancer here, really high in Asia. Why are they high in Asia? What happens in Asia that will give you high rates of stomach and liver cancer as opposed to anywhere else? And we're going to think about different geographic variations of infections as well. Similarly, with nasopharyngeal cancers. These are particularly prevalent in Hong Kong. So what's going on there? Why are they high in Hong Kong but really low in the UK? What's the environmental or genetic factors that contribute to that? So is it genetics or environment? Well, it's probably a combination of those things, and there have been studies which have shown that. So for example, post-World War II, when a lot of Japanese migrants moved to the US Instead of developing stomach cancer, which would be more common in Japan, they started to develop more breast cancer. So that suggests there's something environmental. There's something that they're doing in the US, something in the environment that is perhaps predisposing them more to breast cancer and the converse in Japan for stomach cancer. But we also have a lot of genetic variation within the population, right? And I mentioned those BRCA mutation carriers. So within a population, of course, you will have some people who are genetically predisposed.
blocks.topicLabel: Cancer development, environmental risks, and epidemiological patterns

blocks.label: Pathogens and viral mechanisms in cancer
blocks.content: So what environmental cancers might be involved in this process? So we'll come back to the roulette wheel, and we're going to start thinking about some of those environmental exposures, and I'm going to start with infectious agents. So can pathogens drive cancer? And sometimes you hear these stories, right? "Oh, my uncle went down with a really bad flu, and then he got cancer." Was it really caused by the infection, or was it an incidental finding? So what's the evidence? Well, there are a number of pathogens which are associated with different cancers. One of the ones which is really highlighting here is Helicobacter pylori. And of course, you all know the story of Barry Marshall, the crazy Australian guy who drank Helicobacter pylori and got stomach ulcers. Well, that chronic inflammation can perhaps evolve into something more sinister, such as stomach cancer, and actually, we think there are also proteins produced by the bacteria that may also play a role, and there's a nice lecture on that if you do part two pathology. We know that Epstein-Barr virus is isolated from Burkitt lymphoma cells, cancer of the immune system. So it suggests maybe they're playing a role, and we'll come on to that, too. We know that people who are infected with helminths, such as schistosomiasis, are at a higher rate of bladder cancer. So that suggests there's some link there, too, and again, could this be down to chronic inflammation? Because if you have chronic inflammation and that's causing a constant sort of battle with reactive oxygen species and cells proliferating, maybe that's also part of this conducive microenvironment that allows cells with mutations to grow out. Another example is with fungus. So Aspergillus is particularly associated with liver cancer, and that's because Aspergillus produces a toxin that's mutagenic, and I'm going to talk about that as well. But viruses in particular are associated with many different cancers, and the mechanisms these viruses use vary. So cervical cancer, of course, all females in this country are vaccinated against HPV, the reason being to protect against cervical cancer, and that's because, of course, these high-risk papillomaviruses have proteins which interfere with our normal cell cycle regulatory control proteins, such as p16. So these viruses can interrupt the cell cycle. They can prevent those normal cell cycle control processes from occurring, and of course, then you'll have cells which are proliferating when they shouldn't be, which of course may then pick up more mutations. We're going to talk a bit more later about EBV and also HPV, but another example is Kaposi sarcoma, and we see Kaposi sarcoma in patients who are HIV positive. And what we think is happening there is that transient immunosuppression allows human herpes virus 8 infection, and that this is driving this very unique form of cancer, Kaposi sarcoma. And then we have the integrating retroviruses. So HTLV, human T-lymphotropic virus type 1, we see that in very specific cases of T-cell leukemia, particularly in Asian populations. And that's an integrating virus. So you can imagine that if the retrovirus integrates its genome into the promoter of a tumor suppressor gene or an oncogene, or it can affect in some way protein expression and cell cycle control, that can also play a role in driving mutagenic processes.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Burkitt lymphoma etiology, malaria, and Myc translocation
blocks.content: So I'm going to use the example of Burkitt lymphoma, because this is a really interesting story. And Burkitt lymphoma is named after this Irish surgeon, this guy here, Denis Burkitt, who spent a lot of time traveling across Africa. He lived in Kampala for a while, in Uganda, and he noticed these children. And being a surgeon, he was quite interested in this, but he noticed these children with these large swellings in their jaw. And originally, he thought this was a bone cancer, a sarcoma. And he isolated cells from these tumors, and he happened to be giving a talk about these tumors back in London, and there was a guy called Anthony Epstein in the audience. And Anthony Epstein was saying, "Well, maybe there's a virus there." So he sent him some of the cells from these children in Uganda, and sure enough, what did Epstein do? Him and Yvonne Barr isolated the Epstein-Barr virus. So this was the first time that someone had shown a virus can be implicated in the development of a cancer. He was quite a pioneer of the cancer field because he was also the first person to show that chemotherapy could be used to treat cancer, and he was treating children with Burkitt lymphoma with methotrexate in his kitchen in Kampala. So this eventually became recognized as a lymphoma rather than a sarcoma, and this entity named after him, Burkitt lymphoma, was formalized in 1963. And this was back in the day when you could publish in eminent journals like The Lancet as a single author, and he described these very distinct cancers. Now, he wasn't content with just knowing that there were these cancers. He also wanted to understand a little bit more about what was going on. So he traveled across Africa when he was doing his missionary work, and he particularly traveled across this sort of region here. And he mapped that this was where he was seeing all the cases of this very distinct jaw tumor, this Burkitt lymphoma. And you could see that it was in a very defined area, which he called the lymphoma belt. So a minimum temperature of 60 degrees Fahrenheit, a yearly rainfall of greater than 50 mils, and regions 10 degrees to the north and south of the equator. Very specific. So this starts you thinking, well, actually, maybe these are environments that favor infectious agents, favor the propagation of certain infectious agents. And indeed, when you look at the malaria map, there is almost a complete identical overlap. Aha, the plot thickens. So not only are we perhaps getting this cancer in populations which have large incidences of chronic malaria, ongoing, multiple infections with malaria, but they also have EBV in their tumor cells. And this is our current thinking. Again, even all these years later, we don't still fully understand what might be going on. But the general idea is that, of course, we all have EBV infection, and we tend to get it very early in life, and it goes into latency, and we don't know we've had it. And you know, of course, that if you get EBV infection a bit later in life, when you're a teenager, you then develop glandular fever or mono or kissing disease, whatever you want to call it. So we all have latent EBV infection. Now, imagine a situation where you then develop malaria, and we also see Burkitt lymphoma in patients with HIV. Could it be the case that that latent EBV infection is in some way then activated because we're losing the T cells that would normally control that? So we get this enhanced proliferation of B cells in the germinal center driven by EBV, and this germinal center expansion causes rapid cell proliferation, B cell proliferation. And what are those cells doing at that time in the germinal center? Well, they're rearranging their heavy chains. They're expressing Myc because they're proliferating, and both of those genes are being transcribed at the same time. So there's a greater propensity that when those genes get put back together following replication and transcription and translation, they get put back in the wrong places, and you end up with this random chromosomal translocation event where you juxtapose the heavy chain enhancer regions to Myc. So Myc gets switched on permanently in these highly proliferative B cells. And of course, what we end up here with is Burkitt lymphoma. So a combination of the environment being just right, transient immunosuppression due to malaria, reactivation of EBV, rapid proliferation, pick up a mutation, which in this case is a translocation and outgrowth of those cells.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Dietary toxins and UV radiation mechanisms
blocks.content: Okay, so we can have infectious agents involved in the development of cancer. What about diet? We know that in the US, there are very high rates of colorectal cancer. Is it their diet? And of course, you read lots of things. You read about well-cooked meat. Don't overcook your barbecue meat. Don't eat bacon. All these sort of things you hear about in the press. Could diet be doing something? Are there carcinogens present in some of our foodstuffs? Well, I'm first going to go back to the example of the fungus. And this fungus particularly grows on peanuts in warm, humid environments. And it produces this naturally occurring toxin called aflatoxin. And so particularly in regions of Asia, where this is a huge part of the diet, there is chronic exposure to aflatoxin. And this is what aflatoxin looks like. I don't want you to remember the structure of aflatoxin, but of course, through your chemistry, you'll know that there are lots of these benzene rings, and there are lots of these reactive groups attached to it. And that looks a lot like a DNA base, right? So what can happen is that these reactive aryl hydrocarbon structures can form adducts with DNA. Now, this particular one, aflatoxin, isn't reactive. But when we eat it, and if it moves through to our liver, in our livers, there are oxidases. And what those oxidases do is convert aflatoxin into an epoxide derivative. So it has this oxygen group added, and this is what makes it reactive. Now it can bind to DNA bases, in particular guanine. And of course, if you have this bulky adduct on your DNA, that's going to affect how your DNA is transcribed. And it's going to also lead to mutations, because when we have replication, maybe your cell won't see this bulky adduct as being a guanine anymore. So there are some naturally occurring compounds which are mutagenic as well that are in our diet. What about UV light? What does UV light do? Well, UV light is a form of radiation, so energy transfer. And what happens with that UV radiation is that we end up with these thymine dimers forming between thymine bases on the same strand. And so you can imagine that if you have these thymine dimers forming, again, that's going to affect DNA replication. And we have nucleotide excision repair, and for the most part, that nucleotide excision repair will deal with those dimers. But of course, the more you expose yourselves to this radiation, UV radiation, the higher the chance that some of those maybe won't be repaired and could lead to acquisition of mutations. So where are we now?
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, AhR metabolism, and DNA adducts
blocks.content: Smoking cigarettes. So why are cigarettes so bad for you? I mean, they don't smell nice. We all know that. They're really quite horrible things. But what's in them that causes cancer? Well, there are lots of chemicals in them. But one thing in particular, again, are these polycyclic hydrocarbons, so these benzene rings that we see. And it also so happens that these polycyclic hydrocarbons are also present in well-cooked meat. And in particular, there's one called benzo[a]pyrene. And benzo[a]pyrene on its own isn't too much of a problem, but again, it's something that we can convert in our bodies into a carcinogen, and it has indirect effects on DNA. And exposure to this has been associated with a wide variety of cancers, including lung cancers and colon cancers. So I just, again, put this in from the popular press. Yes, bacon really is killing us. Now, of course, if you read the popular press, you wouldn't eat or do anything. Of course, we do have repair mechanisms, so hopefully those repair mechanisms will deal with any damage that's caused. So if you want a bacon sandwich, go ahead and have your bacon sandwich. Maybe the question here is whether you have it every day. So what happens with these particular compounds, with these benzo[a]pyrenes? So benzo[a]pyrene, as I said, it has this multi-ring benzene ring structure. And what it does is when it enters the cells, it binds to a protein called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. Now, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor is part of our normal metabolic pathway to detoxify, and we see it in the liver, for example, in liver cells, but also in other cells. And when it binds the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, it then enables that hydrocarbon receptor to bind to this protein here, ARNT, or aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator. And as the name suggests, this then enables the aryl hydrocarbon receptor to move into the nucleus, where it can bind to promoter regions called xenobiotic response elements, and it drives transcription of one enzyme in particular, and that's a liver enzyme called CYP1A1. Now, what CYP1A1 does is it converts this sort of unreactive aryl hydrocarbon structure into this epoxide by adding this oxygen group here, and that is what can form adducts with DNA. So sometimes it's our own bodily processes which are there to detoxify, but rather paratoxically create mutagens. So bulky adducts can form in all of these cases, and in particular on guanine residues. So you can see how this reactive oxygen here goes off, it makes water, and you end up with this amine group being replaced with this big, bulky structure. So you can imagine if you have this big, bulky structure attached to guanine in your DNA, it's going to affect replication and transcription. And the way that this may work with many of these compounds is that essentially they get bound to guanines or adenines. In this case, I'm showing you an adenine. So you get this bulky adduct sticking out of the DNA, and so when it comes to replication, it's not matched correctly with the appropriate base. And that's because it's not seen as being the adenine that we think it is. And so perhaps it's now looking more like a thymine, and so our replication machinery puts an adenine there instead. And so what we end up with are these transversions. And these transversions, of course, may change the DNA code, and if they occur in really important sequences of introns, for example, that encode really important parts of key proteins, they may go on to have a deleterious effect. This is another example of one of those compounds. So this is TCDD. TCDD was responsible for a lot of cancers that occurred in the Vietnamese population after the Vietnamese War. And that's because they used a really nasty form of warfare, which is using this herbicide called Agent Orange to kill off the food supply. And that ended up tainting all the food, what was left, with this TCDD. And TCDD, again, is one of these benzyl ring structures which can affect how our DNA responds. And again, it has indirect effects on DNA and is also associated with lots of birth defects. Now, in the case of TCDD, it's not converted by any enzymes in our bodies. Instead, what we think TCDD does is it binds again to that aryl hydrocarbon receptor, which produces the CYP1A1. But a byproduct of CYP1A1 activity is the production of reactive oxygen species and lots of oxidative stress. And of course, that can cause DNA damage and inflammation, which again provides us with an environment conducive with the acquisition of mutations and outgrowth of clones of cells.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Tissue-specific activation of carcinogens in the bladder
blocks.content: So where do we come to now? Back to cigarette smoke. So back to cigarette smoke. There are also other compounds in there, and there are other things such as aromatic amines. So this is beta-naphthylene. You see it's got this amine group on the benzene rings. And now this is another compound that has to be activated by xenobiotic metabolism. And in particular, we see it happen in people that have bladder cancer. Not other cancers, they get bladder cancer. So what is it about the bladder environment that makes this compound particularly carcinogenic there? So there are some tissue specific carcinogens out there. So normally, beta-naphthylene undergoes hydroxylation, and then it very rapidly gets glycosylated. And that's great because then it's deactivated. This is the carcinogenic form with this reactive oxide hydroxide group there. So it gets glycosylated and it's no longer carcinogenic. And this happens in all cells of the body except in the bladder. Because in the bladder, we have glucuronidase, and this is in humans and dogs. And what that glucuronidase does is it converts it back to that reactive derivative. And so therefore, it's specifically carcinogenic in the bladder. So there's tissue specificity to some of these as well. Some of them have to be activated by xenobiotic processes. Some of them are inherently active but maybe drive chronic inflammation. So there are lots of things going on.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Asbestos and chronic inflammation as tumor promotion
blocks.content: There are also environmental exposures which we associate with cancer, and I mentioned at the beginning asbestos. Now, there's no evidence that asbestos fibers cause DNA damage. So how are people presenting with a very specific type of lung cancer? And of course, this happened a lot to people like carpenters, were working with these boards of asbestos, maybe back in the '50s. They were being used as building materials. They were sawing through them. They were breathing in the fibers. But we know the fibers don't cause DNA damage. So what do they do? And they cause a very specific type of lung cancer, it's a cancer of the mesothelium, not a cancer of the lung tissue itself. So the mesothelial lining of the lung. And we think what happens here is that those small fibers, they're so small that when they're inhaled, they penetrate through the lung, they lodge themselves in the mesothelium, and here they just drive chronic inflammation. So they're not acting as mutagens directly, but they're creating an environment where there's chronic inflammation going on. So how might that chronic inflammation be leading to cancer? Is it essentially having an adjuvant effect? And of course, what happens when we have chronic inflammation? Of course, this is a very simplistic cartoon of what you've been learning in your immunology lectures. But we know production of reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, is part of an inflammatory response. That can cause DNA damage. We also know there are lots of cytokines being produced and growth factors which may drive certain cells to grow out of control, not least of which inflammatory cells, which can develop into cancers called lymphomas. So we consider this to be promoter activity rather than initiator. So we think that maybe there are clones of cells sat there which are primed with having mutations in key genes, but they don't have the right microenvironment, which asbestos then provides by causing this chronic inflammation. So not all cancers, not all mutagens have direct activity on DNA. Some of them we instead consider to be promoters rather than initiators.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: The Berenbaum two-stage model: initiators versus promoters
blocks.content: And this was the first study that really gave rise to this idea. This is the Berenbaum hypothesis. So what they did was they took something, a mutagen that they called the initiator, and this mutagen happens to be a compound called DMBA. Very reactive, it's mutagenic. And they painted it onto the skin of mice. And when they just put the mutagen, the mice didn't develop skin cancer. So just having the mutagen on its own wasn't sufficient for cancer development. But when they followed it up with something which they called a promoter, they then did develop tumors. And equally, if they did it the other way around, they didn't get tumors. So not only have we got the mutagen, but we've got something that's a promoter. So what was that promoter? Well, that was something called TPA, 12-O-tetradecanoyl phorbol 13-acetate. Why would this be a promoter? What does this do? So we have the initiator, the mutagen DMBA, and we have the promoter TPA. Now, this is what TPA looks like, and it's this bit in the red lines there. That's TPA. And actually, what this whole molecule is here is something called diacylglycerol. Now, diacylglycerol is a very important part of cell signaling pathways in our cells. And what TPA can do is mimic diacylglycerol. And TPA is, again, another naturally occurring compound. It's present in croton oil, which is often used as a herbal medicine. So again, we often think things like herbal medicines are safe, but sometimes they themselves contain carcinogens, and this is one example of that. And this is basically an agonist for protein kinase C. So what I want you to look at here is the fact that normally, diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C, but its production is very much controlled by external signals, growth factors, for example. And that activates protein kinase C that then initiates this whole plethora of activities within cells. So what happens in the case of phorbol esters like TPA is that they mimic diacylglycerol, activate PKC independently of these external signals, and drive cell proliferation. And there are, of course, drugs we now have that can inhibit these pathways that we use to treat cancer, and we'll come onto those in the last lecture. So we have mutagens and we have promoters. And this will become important in the next lecture that I give to you as well because there's a more relevant example now that I'm going to talk about with lung cancer. So promoters essentially cause cell turnover, inflammation perhaps. And actually, cigarette smoke might be one of those really bad things because it can do both of those things. Not only does it contain mutagens, but it also causes inflammation. Asbestos, we think that's just happening as a promoter, sorry, as a, yeah, as a promoter, not an initiator. So not all causes of cancer are potentially due to mutagens which are causing DNA damage, but also processes which provide the right microenvironmental environment for those cells to be able to evolve, to grow, to predominate.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Developmental timing and tissue susceptibility to alkylating agents
blocks.content: Okay, so we have choices. We have random events that we can't do anything about. We maybe have bad luck events which are a consequence of that. And we have lots of environmental exposures which we can do things about. We can reduce our exposure to these things. We can try and live a healthy lifestyle so that we're not under chronic inflammation. And now I want to think about the cell host of those mutations as well, because as well as a conducive microenvironment and inflammation permitting that growth, what if also there are agents which are specifically acting in certain cell types due to what those cells are doing at any stage during development? And here we're going to talk about alkylating agents. So this is an alkylating agent. This is NMU or N-nitroso N-methylurea, and this is prevalent in fermented foods. And we see a lot of exposure to alkylating agents, particularly in Africa, in regions where we see high rates of esophageal cancer. And this has been associated with eating fermented foods such as salted fish, but also with taking extremely hot drinks. And so, of course, the idea there would be that there is a mutagen, this alkylating agent present in that salted fish, and that these extremely hot drinks cause DNA damage and inflammation, which together increases the risk of developing esophageal cancers. And what it does is it transfers its methyl group, leading to these AT to GC transitions. But the reason I'm bringing this up is because it can act on very specific stages of cells in different organs. And actually, MNU is much more mutagenic when you inject it into young female rats as opposed to adults or male rats. So why is that the case? And actually, what these rats develop are mammary tumors. So these are the mammary glands of the rat, and you can see that they're really swollen here. So they've developed into tumors. And of course, what's happening at this stage of life? So these are rats which are going through puberty. So the tissue in the mammary gland is restructuring, it's redeveloping at that time. So perhaps therefore, there are some tissues which are prone or predisposed to picking up mutations from different agents because they're actively proliferating at the time they're exposed. And actually, we do see that in humans as well. There are examples, for example, when survivors of the Japanese atomic bomb, most of the cancers that we saw developed in teenagers who were exposed, and particularly young girls who were exposed to the atomic bomb at a very important part of their life, when they're going through puberty. So there are some stage of life specific activities which may also contribute to cancer development. Another example here is that it's been shown that if you compare the rate of breast cancer in childless women, and we put that at one, and then compare it to the rates of breast cancer in women who have their first pregnancy at different ages, and you can see women that have children much younger in life, much younger than we would perhaps do here, are protected against breast cancer. So there's clearly something very specific about certain stages of life when it comes to some cancers, and the availability of potentially hormones that might also be driving this process. So DNA damage underlies cancer development. Sometimes this damage is caused directly by mutagens. Sometimes there's also a contributing indirect mechanism, such as chronic inflammation. We know that DNA can be damaged in a number of ways. So not only by natural mutagens such as aflatoxin, but there are also chemicals that we are exposed to that play a role. Some of those chemicals are inert unless they're converted by xenobiotic metabolism in our bodies into toxic derivatives. And some act more as promoters rather than initiators, as we see in the case of asbestos. And then finally, some mutagens require specific environments or specific stages of life, such as MNU in pubertal rats. And in some cases, such as beta-naphthyl in the example I gave you, it's only converted back into this carcinogen in the bladder. So there are some tissue specificities as well to these cancer causes.
blocks.topicLabel: Specific biological and chemical mechanisms of carcinogenesis

blocks.label: Mutational signatures and genomic profiling
blocks.content: So how can we work out what's causing cancer? We do the epidemiology. We can make lots of models in the lab, and we can come up with ideas and hypotheses. But how can we prove that cancer cells were exposed to any particular carcinogen? So of course, these days we have the ability to do very high throughput DNA sequencing, whole genome sequencing, and as the cost of that comes down, the more cancer genomes we've been able to sequence. And what you can do is you can work out patterns of mutations in your DNA sequences. So for example, here we're looking at C to A transitions, and we're looking at them in the context of the DNA sequence. And so you can look at the DNA code in a cancer cell and work out these sort of patterns of the type of changes we're seeing in DNA and the context in which they occur and how many of them you see. And you can relate this back to studies where they've exposed normal cells to carcinogens to develop these signatures. So this is some work that was done here in Cambridge, not by me, but by others. And this shows patterns of DNA mutations associated with exposure to different carcinogens. And of course, you can't read that. So I'm going to zoom in on three of those that relate to things we've been talking about today. Alkylating agents. I've got the wrong glasses on. Reactive oxygen species, and at the top there, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. And you can instantly see there are different patterns of mutations that are caused by exposure to these agents. So we can go to cancer cells, and we can map up these patterns to what we're seeing in the cancer cells, and we can then say, "Well, maybe that cancer was caused because that person was exposed to a particular carcinogen." Of course, it's not quite that simple, and you do see mixtures of lots of different signatures in cancer cells, but it enables us to have some idea.
blocks.topicLabel: Methodologies for identifying and proving carcinogenicity

blocks.label: Biobanks, epidemiology, and in vivo animal testing
blocks.content: So how can we prove carcinogenicity? How do we prove it? And of course, it's unethical for me to take a group of people and expose you all to a carcinogen and wait and see if you get cancer. So ultimately, we can only work with epidemiological studies. And we can also feed these compounds to mice and rats, which some of you may still consider unethical. But these are the things that we have in our arsenal. And we can also do, we can replace mice and rats to some extent by doing in vitro assays. But bear in mind, a lot of what I've told you about those carcinogens also depend on the body environment. So we're not going to see in vitro that they have carcinogenic potential, hence the in vivo studies. So epidemiology, I introduced the lecture with some epidemiology, and that works really well. We can associate causes with cancers when we can clearly separate the exposed population from the non-exposed. So for example, that's smoking and lung cancer. Clearly, people who smoke cigarettes have a higher risk of lung cancer. But of course, you also get lung cancer in non-smokers, so it's not as clear cut. But there's a lot of strong evidence there. It's also a very specific type of cancer, it's lung cancer. It's not other types of cancer that we see. So again, this tells us that there's something very specific about that exposure. And what we can do is we can also develop biomarkers to monitor exposure to different things. So all those chemicals that cause DNA adducts, they're often excreted in the urine, those DNA adducts. And so what you can do is you can survey a population by looking for the presence of these DNA adducts in the urine and see if a population is being exposed to these products. And so there are good examples, as we've talked about today. You've got asbestos and mesothelioma, you've got occupational exposure to aromatic amines and bladder cancer, smoking and squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus, and then that example of aflatoxin exposure with liver cancer. And actually, these people also have a high rate of HBV infection. So we think that may also be playing a role in this promotional activity, this chronic inflammation. So how do you do these studies? Well, you go to biobanks, and in the UK, it's one of the largest biobanks that's available in the world. There are also some very good biobanks in the Nordic countries. But what happened in the UK was they enrolled about 500,000 individuals at about 40 to 69 years of age, bearing in mind that cancer in general occurs in an older population, although we're seeing a shift in that now. And they got these people to fill out health and lifestyle questionnaires. They collected blood, urine, saliva. They sequenced their DNA. And you can request samples from the biobank, and you can go ahead and explore your hypothesis from those samples. What about the mouse studies? Well, these are a little bit more difficult. So generally, everything that we eventually put into our mouths, whether it be a drug or something else, generally has gone through some sort of toxicological study. And the way we do that is we expose animals. Normally, we have to go through at least two different species for up to two years, and we expose them to the maximum tolerated dose of a compound, and we look and see if there's any toxicity, if they develop cancers. But of course, this is quite inhumane. It's very expensive. We only see about 70% concordance between mouse and rat, for example. But also remember, some of those carcinogens are only carcinogenic in humans and dogs, that one I gave you, so you would miss it in a mouse or a rat study. So it's not foolproof, but it can give us an idea if we have some carcinogenic activity. But also, for some of these carcinogens, the maximum tolerated dose is huge. So back in my life, I was involved in a study where we were trying to work out if saccharin, so sweeteners in these drinks, does that cause cancer? And we were feeding rats tons and tons of saccharin in their food, but they didn't develop cancer. But it has been linked with some cancers, so there's clearly something going on there, but we're certainly not seeing that in mice and rats. And you have to feed them a lot. So I'd have to be drinking gallons of Coke every day, gallons and gallons to see mutations in my DNA. So there's also the issue of the dose that we're exposed to. And for many things, we're probably not exposed to enough of it in high enough doses to worry about it. And actually, even some common fruits and vegetables contain toxins. We still eat them. Maybe they do have an effect, maybe they don't, but we don't die of them. And so the amount of toxin we're exposed to may also play a role.
blocks.topicLabel: Methodologies for identifying and proving carcinogenicity

blocks.label: In vitro Ames tests and risk-benefit considerations
blocks.content: So we can do epidemiology, we can do in vivo studies, and I also mentioned that in vitro assay. So this is something called the Ames test. It's the workhorse of toxicology in many ways. And what you do here is you take a bacterial strain, and this is a bacterial strain that requires histidine for growth. So it only grows when you give it histidine, and it's been mutated so that it cannot produce its own histidine. And what you do is then you expose those bacteria to your mutagen, and then you plate them out, and if they've reverted to a his-positive phenotype so that they then can produce their own histidine, they'll grow out, and you can say that your compound has some sort of mutagenic activity. And you can go one step further than that in that you can put rat liver extract, which is enriched in these xenobiotic enzymes, these P450 enzymes. So you can also look at compounds which maybe are only mutagenic when they are metabolized. Now, of course, this is sort of like the bog standard for testing carcinogenicity, but as I said, we have to be aware of potency. But of course, what we now know of cancer biology is that these tests are woefully inadequate because they don't incorporate all the other things that go on in our bodies that may be permissive of cancer growth. And I talked about that really important role of the immune system, but not just that, angiogenesis, growth factors, stroma, all these other things which can contribute to make something have carcinogenic properties. So ultimately, it's all about the risks versus the benefits. We know that medical X-rays can cause DNA damage, but you need to know if you have a broken bone. Some of you may think having a nice suntan is worth the risk. Do you want skin cancer? Do you want a suntan? We make these decisions every day in our life. Some things we don't decide we want to use them, such as herbicides, and we don't know there are carcinogens in them, but we hope that the government will act on these things and ban all these dangerous agents. So we will end it there with this summary, that much cancer is environmental, including lifestyle-related factors. Working out what is carcinogenic is actually quite challenging. Working out the potency of carcinogens is even more challenging. And ultimately, there's this benefit/risk analysis that we all take every day in our lives. [audience applauding]
